Mid season; I can safely judge production and disease resistance and flavor by now. Keep in mind I'm in a mediterranean climate in the Pacific NW, moderately hot, dry summers but STEADY heat. It's not 60 one day and 105 the next, unlike continental climates. Fall and spring are VERY rainy and very cool, temps tend to max out in the upper 50s from March through early June at least.

Big Beef - I had high hopes and the flavor fell hugely short, they're not bad just not worth the home grow effort IMO. Disease resistance is good. Very virile plants grew fast and took off immediately, seems well suited to the single string trellis method. Yield was good, I'd say 6.5/10. Not bad but there are definitely more productive plants for this climate. Overall not worth it here. YouTuber mhpgardener said they were really good in his climate in I believe Alabama or somewhere else in the southeast. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Italian Ice - Yield good, probably 7/10 for cherry tomato plants. These took forever to germinate and grew verrrrry slowly until the dry summer heat hit. Maybe good for a very hot climate? No issues with disease but the leaves are a little pale and nothing seems to fix that, I might need a soil pH adjustment... Taste is very low acid but sweet and very tomatoey. Note these did not really grow white, mostly a very pale yellow. You can definitely eat them while they're white but they're not as sweet at that point. Worth a regrow if I have the room!

Bush Early Girl - These are determinate but still have a good yield. Definitely an ideal container candidate. Medium acidity. Taste that's somewhere between good and very good. Not amazing but definitely good. No issues with disease again at all, these plants were really resistant to leaf curl which affected all of the other plants, although a small amount of leaf curl is not bad at all, just a minor stress response to dry summer heat and sometimes wind. These are worth growing if you want to stake them with one of those garden store 3 foot cages or in a 5-10 gallon bucket.

Kellogg's Breakfast - I didn't start these myself so I can't comment on germination. They do have a little bit of an issue with bacterial and/or fungal spot on the leaves that none of my other plants had but that was started by lazy beaners in a greenhouse somewhere. It's hard to fully control but consistent weekly applications of copper fungicide kept it from spreading. No saving the branches that already had the spots though. The taste is completely unique. It's almost not even tomatoe-y, I know this sounds retarded but the closest thing I can think to compare it to is kind of a generic breakfast cereal grain taste. Or if you've ever tasted horse grain... (I will not submit to further questioning about that). Grew very tall, tried to throw tons of suckers that I had to repeatedly pull off, still doing it after I cut the top at about 7.5 feet. Medium yield, maybe 5/10. Could definitely be better, I THINK our summer heat has stopped many of the flowers from setting fruit. Worth a regrow in the distant future, not a huge fan of the flavor but it's not a bad plant to grow and still tastes good. Perhaps better suited to some place where the summer temperature stays 85-90 and below? Took hold VERY well in our cool slightly wet early summer though.
